title: Strain rate, and temperature dependent flow behavior and microstructure evolution of FeMnNiCo and (FeMnNiCo) 95 Mo 5  high-entropy alloys
abstract: Abstract In this work, the effect of strain rate (10 −1 –10 3  s −1 ), temperature (77 and 293 K) and Mo addition on the compressive flow stress behavior and microstructure evolution of the fcc single-phase FeMnNiCo and (FeMnNiCo) 95 Mo 5  high entropy alloy systems was investigated. A detailed study performed by SEM and TEM revealed that, in addition to dislocation gliding, mechanical twinning occurred during the deformation. The addition of 5 at.% of Mo increases yield strength while decreasing the stacking fault energy in the fcc alloy, thereby enhancing its tendency to form twins. This deformation was particularly promoted at low temperatures and high strain rates. The mechanical testing was complemented by detailed microstructural characterization in order to establish the relationship between strain rate, temperature, deformation mechanisms, and microstructural evolution.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: High entropy alloys (HEAs) have attracted much attention due to their unique microstructures and excellent properties including high strength, good deformability and fracture toughness, exceptional hardness, superior oxidation resistance, and corrosion resistance[ 1 ,  2 ,  3 – 4 ]. Since the pioneering studies of Cantor et al. [ 5 ] and Yeh et al. [ 6 ], the number of alloy systems classified as HEAs has rapidly expanded encompassing a broad range of chemical compositions and crystal structures. Owing to multiple strengthening mechanisms such as solid-solution hardening, and deformation twinning associated with relatively low stacking fault energies, many HEAs exhibit excellent mechanical properties even at cryogenic conditions[ 1 ,  7 ]. Among the various HEA systems, the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi Cantor alloy has become one of the most extensively studied model materials. Its mechanical behavior has been shown to be strongly dependent on strain rate and temperature. Recently, Huang et al. [ 8 ] reviewed the strain-rate sensitivity of HEAs and demonstrated that Cantor alloy showed a pronounced strain rate dependence in both strength and work-hardening behavior. Li et al. [ 9 ] showed that deformation twinning is the main mechanism in this face-centered cubic (fcc) HEA at high strain rates and low temperatures. Similarly, Qiao et al. [ 10 ] investigated the strain rate effect of the Cantor alloy in quasi-static and dynamic tensile tests at strain rates of up to approximately 7× 10 3  s −1  and showed that the high work-hardening capability suppresses adiabatic shear localization [ 9 ,  11 ]. However, intermediate strain rate regime around 10 2  s −1  has received comparatively little attention [ 9 ] and [ 10 ,  12 ]. In contrast, Park et al. [ 12 ] observed adiabatic shear banding during compression at strain rates of about 4.7 × 10 3  s −1  in tests of CoCrFeMnNi. Tsai et al. [ 13 ] further demonstrated that dislocation glide dominates at lower strain rates, whereas deformation nanotwinning becomes increasingly important at strain rates exceeding 6 × 10 3  s −1 .

Although most studies have focused on the Cantor alloy and its derivatives, a wide variety of alternative HEA systems have also been developed. For instance, refractory HEAs containing Mo have attracted attention because of their high-temperature strength and thermal stability. Mo has also been introduced into Cantor-based alloys to modify their mechanical response and phase stability. Qin et al. added Mo to the Cantor alloy in order to strengthen the fcc matrix [ 14 ], whereas other studies reported that partial replacement of Mn by Mo promotes the formation of intermetallic, µ and σ phases [ 15 ]. More importantly, Mo consistently emerges as a powerful regulator of twinning behavior in HEAs, through its pronounced influence on stacking fault energy (SFE), lattice distortion, and phase stability. In single-crystal CoCrFeNiMo 0.2 , Mo dramatically lowers the SFE, enabling the formation of both nanotwins and macrotwins, particularly at low temperatures such as 77 K, where twinning becomes an energetically favorable deformation mode [ 16 ]. In multicomponent fcc HEAs such as Co 35 Cr 25 Fe 20 Ni 20 , Mo addition directly triggers the TWIP/TRIP effect by reducing SFE and altering charge redistribution, leading to simultaneous activation of deformation twins and HCP lamellae during plastic flow [ 17 ]. These observations indicate that Mo shifts the deformation behavior toward deformation modes dominated by partial-dislocation activity and twin-assisted hardening. Further evidence from Fe 40 Mn 40 Co 10 Cr 10  indicates that Mo acts as a strong SFE reducing element, promoting extensive stacking-fault formation and increasing the likelihood of twin nucleation as SFE approaches low or even negative values [ 18 ]. In electrodeposited or nanocrystalline multi-principal element alloys, Mo causes significant lattice distortion and generates negative SFE regions, which further increases twin activity and supports the nucleation of stacking faults and nanoscale deformation twins under load [ 19 ]. Furthermore, the pronounced lattice distortion introduced by Mo in CoCrFeNi-based HEAs also contributes to higher levels of planar slip and localized stress concentrations, which facilitate twin nucleation during deformation, particularly in compression [ 20 ]. Together, these studies demonstrate that Mo promotes twinning in fcc-based HEAs primarily by lowering SFE to values where partial dislocation dissociation becomes energetically favorable, while simultaneously modifying local structure through lattice distortion, solute interactions, and short-range order. As a result, Mo-containing HEAs often display enhanced twinning activity, an increased tendency for stacking fault formation, and a greater propensity for twin-mediated plasticity across a variety of processing conditions and loading modes.

sections.heading: Materials and methods
paragraphs: Two HEAs with chemical compositions, denoted Mo0 and Mo5, listed in Table  1  were investigated. An induction vacuum furnace was used to produce the ingots, each with a mass of about 1 kg. Further description of heat treatment of the ingot was described in a recent paper [ 23 ]. Table 1 Chemical composition of the investigated alloys, in at. % Alloy Abbrev Fe Mn Ni Co Mo FeMnNiCo Mo0 24.7 24.2 25.5 25.6 0 (FeMnNiCo) 95 Mo 5 Mo5 23.6 22.5 24.2 24.5 5.2

The ingots were hot rolled at 1100 °C with a thickness reduction of 40% and cold rolled (6 passes) with 10% thickness reduction. Cold rolling followed by annealing was employed to ensure a homogeneous and reproducible grain structure for the subsequent mechanical testing. This process was selected based on our previous studies [ 20 ,  22 ], in which the processing conditions and microstructure evolution were investigated in detail. Subsequently, the grain size was set by static recrystallization at different temperatures and times. For the Mo0 and Mo5 alloys, 1070 °C/600s and 1100 °C/600s were used, respectively. Although deformation twinning may locally occur during cold rolling, the final annealing treatment significantly reduced the deformation-induced microstructural heterogeneities. As a result, the investigated samples exhibited a recrystallized microstructure without a significant fraction of retained deformation twins. The different annealing temperatures were dictated by differences in grain growth kinetics. Grain growth in the Mo5 alloy was slower; therefore, annealing at a higher temperature was required. More details can be found in [ 23 ,  24 ].

Compression tests at strain rates of 1.6 × 10 −1  s −1  and 2 × 10 0  s −1  were performed in a servo-hydraulic universal testing machine MTS 810. The displacement was measured by an electro-optical extensometer Rudolph 200XR. Compressive tests were performed at ambient temperature and at 77 K. The cylindrical specimens (6 mm diameter and height) were immersed in liquid nitrogen well before and during the actual test. All the components in contact with the specimen were also immersed or surrounded by liquid nitrogen. The tup (or punch) of the drop weight was not cooled down to 77 K. During the actual test, nearly adiabatic conditions can be assumed. Hence, the heat generated during the test remains within the specimen. The tests were conducted after no more formation of nitrogen gas bubbles near the specimen was visible. Hence, all the load carrying parts were completely cooled down to 77 K. To achieve a higher strain rate of 2 × 10 2  s −1 an instrumented drop tower with a drop weight of 190 kg was used. The drop height was 140 mm, leading to an impact velocity of about 1.6 m s −1 . For force measurement an instrumented tup was used. For tests at room temperature, the electro-optical extensometer was applied for displacement measurements. For tests at cryogenic temperatures a laser Doppler interferometer was used to measure the displacement of the tup near the interface to the specimen. Tests at ambient temperature and the highest strain rate of 3 × 10 3  s −1  were performed in a split Hopkinson pressure bar setup. Early force equilibrium and relative constant strain rates were achieved by pulse shaping. Details of pulse shaping in a similar split Hopkinson pressure bar device can be found in [ 25 ]. In order to investigate the developed microstructure during dynamic straining, interrupted tests in the drop tower and the split Hopkinson pressure bar were performed with the help of stop rings around the specimens. The effective area suddenly increases when the specimen is compressed to the height of the stop ring made of high-speed steel and, consequently, the ring carries most of the load but deforms only elastically.

The initial microstructures as well as the microstructures at different degrees of deformation were analyzed by means of scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). After grinding and polishing, electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) was applied to investigate the grain orientations and, hence, the twin boundaries. A FEI Nova NanoSEM 450 scanning microscope (SEM) using the Velocity EBSD detector from EDAX was applied. After wire cutting, the center of the compression specimen was analyzed at a voltage of 20 kV, a spot size of 6 and a step size of 0.2 µm. Detailed microstructural characterization was carried out by Tecnai G2 Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM) equipped with energy dispersive X-ray microanalyzer (EDX). Thin foils for TEM were prepared with TenuPol-5 double-jet jet.
electropolishing machine using an electrolyte of perchloric acid (vol. 20%) and methanol (vol. 80%).

sections.heading: The initial alloys
paragraphs: The initial microstructures of both investigated alloys are shown in Fig.  1 . Both materials, independently of Mo content, show coarse microstructure with polygonal grains with annealing twins (Figs.  1 a,b). The twins were identified as annealing twins based on both the processing history and their morphology. They were observed after the annealing treatment, during which recrystallization and grain growth occurred. Furthermore, the twins are relatively thick and located within recrystallized grains, which is characteristic of annealing twins rather than deformation twins. Whereas, the grain size was measured without considering the annealing twins. To ease the discussion of microstructure/property relationships, the materials were processed to exhibit a comparable grain size distribution, thereby minimizing the influence of microstructural variability on material behavior. This approach enabled a more accurate evaluation of the specific effect of molybdenum on the studied properties. Figure 1 a ,  b  EBSD maps showing the initial microstructure of Mo0 and Mo5 alloys, the insets present the grain size distribution;  c ,  d  high-energy X-ray diffraction patterns of Mo0 and Mo5 and  e ,  f  (111), (200), (220) pole figures for Mo0 and Mo5 alloys, respectively.

The diffraction patterns shown in Figs.  1 c, d indicate that both materials in their initial state are characterized solely by single-phase fcc crystal structure, with no evidence of precipitate formation. The additional lower intensity peaks originate from the ordered phase, which intensity decreases or disappears after deformation. This phenomenon will be discussed in the next chapters of this work. The diffraction patterns revealed a shift of the fcc phase intensity peaks toward lower diffraction angles (indicated by the black line in the diffractogram) for the Mo5 alloy. This observation indicates an increase in the lattice parameter caused by the addition of molybdenum. Calculations of the lattice parameter showed that the addition of 5 at.% Mo increased the lattice parameter from 3.5977 Å to 3.6153 Å. Additionally, the analysis of the pole figures for the initial materials reveals the absence of a preferred crystallographic texture, which is characteristic of materials that have undergone annealing following hot deformation (Figs.  1 e, f). This effect is evidenced by the low values of the mrd (multiples of a random distribution) parameter.

sections.heading: Mechanical behavior
paragraphs: The compressive true stress–strain curves obtained at different strain rates (1.6 × 10 −1  s −1  and 2 × 10 0  s −1 , 2 × 10 2 , 3 × 10 3 ) and temperatures (77 and 293 K) for Mo0 and Mo5 are shown in Fig.  2 a and b, respectively. After compressing the samples to a true strain value of 0.4, no cracks were observed in either material, indicating their good plasticity under the applied deformation conditions. In the case of high strain rates, characteristic stress oscillations were observed for both materials. This can be explained by typical inertial effects occurring during SHPB and drop tower testing [ 28 ,  29 ] Figure 2 True stress–strain curves of Mo0 and Mo5 alloys for  a  77 K,  b  293 K in different strain rates.

The interaction between dislocations and solute atoms. Molybdenum, due to the larger atomic radius compared to the other constituent elements, as well as its higher shear modulus, has a considerable influence on the increase in yield strength. This phenomenon can be explained by the reduced dislocation mobility at lower temperatures. When dislocations are pinned at their initial positions by solute atoms, a higher critical shear stress is required to initiate slip. Moreover, the solute atoms themselves act as obstacles to dislocation motion. Considering these factors, it can be concluded that solid-solution strengthening plays an increasingly significant role as the deformation temperature decreases [ 30 ,  31 – 32 ].

In this research, the  m  values for the Mo0 alloy were found to be 0.032 at 293 K and 0.024 at 77 K, while for the Mo5 alloy, they were 0.026 at 293 K and 0.025 at 77 K. At 293 K, the alloy with Mo addition exhibits lower strain-rate sensitivity. Furthermore, it is worth noting that temperature affects the  m  values only in Mo0 alloy, whereas there is almost no difference between m values in Mo5 alloy.

When comparing the obtained values of the strain-rate sensitivity parameter  m  for the Mo0 and Mo5 alloys with compositionally similar HEAs (see Table  2 ), comparable results were observed. However, for the investigated alloys, one would expect the  m  value of the Mo5 alloy to be higher than that of the Mo0 alloy. This expectation arises from the previously discussed effect of Mo addition and its role in increasing the contribution of solid-solution strengthening. A similar.

behaviour can be observed when comparing the CoNiFeNi, Al₀.₁CoCrFeNi, and Al₀.₃CoCrFeNi alloys, where the addition of Al, which, like Mo, is also expected to enhance solid-solution strengthening, leads to an initial decrease in the  m  parameter. Li, in his work [ 42 ], calculated the  m  parameter for CoCrNi and CoCrNiMo 0.2.  In this case the  m  parameter increases with the addition of molybdenum; however, in this alloy, in addition to the solid solution, σ-phase precipitates are present, which affect the SRS behavior. Logically, an increase in the barrier to dislocation motion due to solid-solution strengthening should also result in an increase in strain-rate sensitivity. A similar conclusion was drawn by Adegbite [ 33 ], who suggested that such material behavior warrants further investigation to elucidate how individual alloying elements influence the mechanisms of dislocation motion.

The analysis of the strain-hardening rate as a function of true strain for the investigated materials, tested at various temperatures, is presented in Fig.  4 . Figure 4 Strain-hardening behavior of investigated alloys for  a  Mo0 and  b  Mo5 alloys.

The evolution of the strain-hardening (Eq.  1 ) is typical for this material and can be divided into three characteristic regions. The first region corresponds to an initial linear decrease in the strain-hardening rate. The subsequent increase or stabilization of decreasing trend defines the second region. In the third region, the strain-hardening rate decreases again with increasing strain [ 43 ]. The discussion of the effect of the underlying deformation mechanisms on the shape of the strain-hardening curve will be discussed later.

The activation of individual strengthening mechanisms in a material depends primarily on the value of the stacking fault energy (SFE). Materials with an SFE in the range of approximately 40–20 mJ m −2  [ 44 ] exhibit a tendency to form deformation twins and stacking faults. Materials with lower SFE show an increased propensity for martensitic transformation [ 45 ].

high-entropy alloys, particularly those from the Cantor alloy family, are known to have low SFE, as reported by Liu [ 46 ], with values of 26.5 ± 4.5 mJ m −2  for CoCrNiFeMn and 18 ± 4 mJ m −2  for CoCrNi. The influence of molybdenum on SFE remains not fully understood. Previous studies have reported an SFE of 19 mJ m −2  [ 47 ] for the FeCoCrNiMo₀.₂₃ alloy, compared to 32.5 mJ m −2  for the FeCoCrNi alloy [ 48 ]. Also, Li [ 42 ] [ 49 ] in his research concluded that the addition of Mo should decrease SFE. The deformation mechanisms will be discussed later.

sections.heading: Microstructure and texture
paragraphs: A detailed crystallographic orientation relationship analysis between the twin and the matrix was carried out to investigate the mechanism and conditions associated with the formation of mechanical twins. To illustrate the common twinning plane, a selected region of the IPF-colored maps with Σ3 boundaries and the (111) pole figures were used. This analysis was conducted in one area of the Mo5 alloy deformed at a strain rate of 10 2  s −1  and at room temperature (Fig.  5 ). Figure 5 Selected sections of the inverse pole figure for the Mo5 alloy, together with misorientation profiles and (111) pole figures.

From the obtained misorientation profiles, orientation jumps of approximately 60° were observed, confirming the presence of deformation twins. This phenomenon is associated with a crystal rotation of 60° that occurs during the deformation twinning. The common (111) pole is highlighted in blue, which corresponds well with the trace of the twinning plane K₁. Additionally, the presented (111) pole figures illustrate the change in orientation resulting from a rotation between the matrix and the twin. A characteristic feature of this relationship is the presence of one common plane shared by both the parent and twin orientations.

In Fig.  6 , the microstructures of the studied alloys deformed at different strain rates up to about 0.7 true strain are shown, together with misorientation profiles indicating the number of Σ3 boundaries corresponding to twin boundaries, as well as the relevant pole figures. Σ3 boundaries were determined using 3° tolerance. Figure 6 Inverse pole figure (IPF) maps for theMo0 and Mo5 alloys deformed under different temperatures and strain rates, accompanied by misorientation profiles and pole figures for the (111), (200), and (220) planes.

From the EBSD measurements and misorientation profiles presented in Fig.  6 , it was derived that the formation of twins is affected by temperature and strain rate. The basic relationships from other studies on high entropy alloys, such as [ 9 ], are also found here. At all strain rates, multiple twinning was observed in the present study. Due to large deformation (ε≈0.7), the elongation of the grains is clearly visible. Moreover, there was further twinning within favorably oriented grains. A quantitative analysis of the Σ3 grain boundaries, i.e. the twin planes, reveals a significantly higher amount of twinning after testing at cryogenic temperature. Furthermore, with the addition of Mo, the sensitivity for deformation twinning was increased as indicated by a high twinning density at room temperature and at relatively small strain rates. It is observed that the increase in strain rate affects the increase in number of twin boundaries in the microstructure. The effect of Mo addition on twinning is also visible.

These results correlate directly with the obtained strain-hardening rate (dσ/dε) curves (Fig.  4 ) for these samples, where a continuous decrease in strain-hardening rate is observed during the second stage primarily in the alloy Mo0. Under these conditions, the materials primarily deform by.

dislocation slip. During cryogenic deformation, the fraction of twin boundaries increases. This effect is particularly pronounced under quasi-static deformation conditions, where the proportion of twin boundaries rises on average from 1.1% to approximately 3.7%. With increasing strain rate, the fraction of twin boundaries also increases.

The observed retardation of the strain-hardening rate decrease in samples deformed under cryogenic conditions can likely be attributed to the temperature dependency of activation of the deformation twinning mechanism.

In the Mo5 alloy, the strain-hardening rate curves exhibit a similar overall trend compared to the Mo0 alloy, but a more pronounced retardation in the decrease of the strain-hardening rate can be observed.

These considerations can be directly correlated with the dislocation density and microstrain values derived from synchrotron-based investigations (Fig.  7 ). Figure 7 Dislocation density and lattice microstrain values for the investigated materials under various deformation conditions  a  Mo0,  b  Mo5.

Analysis of the dislocation density for the investigated alloys revealed a characteristic increase with increasing strain and strain rate. The Mo0 alloy exhibits a higher dislocation density compared to Mo5. This difference may be attributed to variations in the annealing procedures prior to.
deformation. The Mo0 alloy was annealed at temperatures approximately 20–30 °C lower than those used for Mo5 due to differences in grain growth kinetics.
For the deformed materials, dislocation density increases, and as expected, it rises with increasing strain rate and decreasing temperature. This trend is observed for all studied alloys. In the.
Mo-containing alloy, the increase in dislocation density is more pronounced under cryogenic.
deformation conditions. This can be explained by the discussed solid-solution strengthening.

Furthermore, as shown previously, Mo addition, cryogenic conditions, and higher strain rates promote deformation twinning. With increasing Mo content, the fraction of twin boundaries also increases, which constitutes an additional barrier to dislocation motion. In other words, twin boundaries can be considered as specific types of grain boundaries. Consequently, a Hall–Petch-like effect occurs [ 50 ], where the effective dislocation path is reduced, requiring a higher.

dislocation density to accommodate the same macroscopic strain. Lattice microstrain values, defined as distortions arising from the crystal lattice deformation, were also analyzed. In the as-received materials, the lowest lattice microstrain values were observed in the (220) plane, whereas the highest were in the (111) plane. After deformation, this trend changes, and the maximum lattice microstrain is observed in the (200) plane. In the initial material, the highest lattice microstrain values were found in Mo0, with a slight decrease observed upon addition of Mo. Although the addition of Mo could be expected to increase lattice distortion and, consequently, lattice microstrain, the opposite trend was observed. This behavior can be attributed to the differences in annealing temperatures (lower for Mo0), which resulted in a lower initial dislocation density. This interpretation is consistent with the well-established relationship between lattice microstrain and dislocation density, where both parameters increase simultaneously during deformation. Furthermore, the highest increase in lattice microstrain was observed for the (200) plane compared to the other analyzed planes. At the same time, Mo addition also affects the lattice microstrain itself. A comparison of the Mo0 and Mo5 alloys shows that, under identical deformation conditions, the Mo5 alloy exhibits significantly higher lattice microstrain values. The analysis of pole figures and EBSD maps for the deformed materials reveals that deformation under compressive loading primarily results in the development of a < 110 > -type fiber texture, as indicated by the intensity maximum in the (220) pole figure oriented parallel to the compression direction. Figure  8  shows the volume fraction of the < 110 > -type fiber texture component, determined within a 15° orientation spread, for the studied materials under different deformation conditions. Figure 8 Volume fraction of the < 110 > -type texture component in the studied materials under different compressive deformation conditions, together with EBSD pole figures of the matrix and twins.

In the initial materials, only minor differences are observed in the volume fraction of the < 110 > texture component, which can be attributed to the previously described variations in material preparation during annealing. The primary purpose of calculating the volume fraction of the < 110 > -type texture component was to estimate differences in the extent of deformation twinning for samples deformed at different strain rates. Since dislocation slip contributes to the formation of the < 110 > component, while twinning drastically reorients the grains leading to so-called texture randomization (weakening), the difference in volume fraction between two different strain rates for the same material can provide an estimate of the relative increase in twin formation at higher strain rates. Such a situation is experimentally illustrated by a single grain shown in Fig.  8  in the EBSD map, where inverse pole figure (IPF) coloring with respect to the compression direction (CD) is applied. In this example, a grain initially oriented with < 110 > parallel to the CD (green color according to the IPF color coding) undergoes reorientation toward the < 112 > direction (purple color). Similar behavior is frequently observed in different regions of the material, as also demonstrated in Fig.  5 . This reorientation contributes to the weakening of the < 110 > texture and enables, to some extent, an estimation of the volume fraction of twinned areas.

For Mo0 alloy deformed at 0.1 s −1  and 10 2  s −1  at room temperature, a decrease in the < 110 > texture fraction of approximately 1% is observed. An increase in strain rate leads to a reduction in the intensity of the < 110 > texture. As previously mentioned, the volume fraction of the texture can be correlated with the occurrence and number of twins in the material’s microstructure. The reduction in the < 110 > texture fraction with increasing strain rate and decreasing temperature is caused by its weakening due to crystal rotations during twinning.

This trend is also evident when considering the Mo addition. Between Mo0 and Mo5, the differences are minor, which is consistent with the analyses of twin boundary fractions (Fig.  6 ), where the number of twin boundaries is slightly higher in the Mo5 alloy.

In summary, at the same strain rates but different deformation temperatures, the decrease in the < 110 > texture fraction is similar for Mo0 and Mo5 alloys. The increase in strain rate leads to a reduction in the intensity of the < 110 > -type fiber texture, which can also be associated with the intensified occurrence of deformation twinning.

The twins are already formed after a small amount of deformation, e.g. after reaching a threshold stress. Hence, the material with Mo5 exhibits higher stress levels due to solid-solution hardening and shows a higher amount of strain-hardening due to easier formation of twins. Similarly, lower temperatures and higher strain rates will increase the strain-hardening in fcc materials. Hence, higher stress levels are reached after smaller deformation.

Microstructural changes after a true compressive strain of about 0.04 of two alloys were investigated by TEM. Figure  9  shows a set of bright-field (BF) images and corresponding selected-area diffraction (SAED) patterns, displayed at their top right, for the materials without and with the addition of Mo deformed at a strain rate of 10 2  s −1  at both 77 K and RT. Moreover, for both specimens of Mo5 alloy, dark-field (DF) images taken from the spots marked by green circles are presented. Surprisingly, quinary alloys (without Mo) do not exhibit nanotwins at both temperatures, while a large amount of dislocations is clearly visible in BF images. In contrast, material Mo5 shows fine nanotwins independently of the deformation temperature, which is confirmed by SAED and DF images. Thus, it can be stated that in the Mo0 alloy, slip deformation is the dominant mechanism, whereas in the Mo5 alloy, twinning plays a significant role. Similar results show. Figure 9 BF and corresponding SAED patterns displayed at their top right for Mo0  a ,  b  and Mo5  c ,  d  as well as  e ,  f  DF images (taken from the red circles marked in SAED) deformed at a strain rate of 10 2  s −1  at 77 K and 293 K, respectively.
samples deformed at static strain rates. However, to draw a valid conclusion, more statistics are needed.
